TESTIMONY IN SUPPORT OF:

May 5, 2025

LD 1635 "An Act to Streamline Municipal Referenda Recount Initiation THE JOINT STANDING COMMITTEE ON STATE AND LOCAL GOVERNMENT

Senator Baldacci, Representative Salisbury, and members of the Committee on
State and Local Government, my name is Amy Arata and I represent House district 104, which includes New Gloucester and part of Gray. It is my pleasure
to present LD 1635, An Act to Streamline Municipal Referenda Recount Initiation.
I have noticed, and perhaps you have as well, that the tone of civic engagement has become rife with hostility and acrimony. This legislation will bring some much-needed relief to a source of strife and mistrust at the local level. As a
former school board member and town budget committee chairman, as well as a legislator, I understand how hard these volunteers work and how discouraging it
is when that work is attacked.
The need for this legislation became apparent to me last year when the school budget referendum in my district, MSAD 15, passed by only 11 votes on June 11.
This upset some members of the community who questioned the validity of the
results, and they had to go through the process of collecting at least 100
registered voters' signatures for a recount. Gathering signatures, especially in a
rural area, is a lot of work. The recount did not occur until July 15, with over a month of uncertainty for the school district and simmering animosity in the community. There was hostility on both sides of the issue, both in town and
especially on social media. Although I had no part in the recount petition drive, I
was present as a community leader and experienced nastiness directed at me. These types of encounters make it difficult for civic leaders to work together on
the common goal of serving our community.

Proudly Serving House District 104
New G1oucester/ Gray (Part)

Regardless of one's hoped-for outcome, most can agree that there is value in certainty that an election result is accurate. LD 1635 would require an automatic
recount if a municipal referendum passes or fails by less than 1% of all votes cast. Although in my district the school budget passed by a small margin, this bill
would also be beneficial for school boards with budgets that fail by a small margin. Before school boards go through the difficult, and sometimes divisive,
work of making budget cuts, they should be sure that the election result was
accurate.
School budgets have not been passing by wide margins in Maine recently. As l
invited legislators to co-sponsor this bill, I sought out representatives of
communities that have had close budget votes. They include towns in Oxford County, Lewiston, Gorham, Westbrook, and Poland. Note that this is a bipartisan
issue. We all want our constituents to be assured that election results are
accurate, and the increased civility that accompanies this certainty.
l believe that 1% is a close enough margin to warrant a recount. My primary
concern is with school budget referenda, but this legislation is in the section of statute that refers to all referenda. If the committee feels that passing this
legislation will result in too many recounts and be a burden on municipal officials
rather than the intended respite, perhaps reducing this threshold to 0.5% of votes cast would alleviate this concern.
Regardless of the details of how the committee chooses to proceed with this legislation, please consider how much this will contribute to progress toward
more trust and civility in local politics. Thank you for your attention and l'm happy to answer questions.
Respectfully,
-
Amy B. Arata

Senator Baldacci, Representative Salisbury and members of the State and Local Government
Committee, my name is Rebecca Lambert, and I am providing updated testimony in opposition to LD 1560 on behalf of the Maine Municipal Association's (MMA) elected 70-member Legislative Policy Committee
(LPC). For reference, MMA is a nonpartisan, nonprofit member service organization and aims to help
provide policy solutions that work for all residents in Maine and the LPC guides the advocacy efforts and establishes positions on bills of municipal interest.
Municipal officials take seriouslythe responsibility to uphold democratic principles and ensure that residents have meaningful opportunities to shape the direction of their communities. Local referendum processes are a vital part of that system, and local leaders support their thoughtful use. However, this bill imposes a one-size-fits-all approach that risk disrupting well-established and locally tailored systemsalready functioning with integrity, transparency, and accountability.
Maine is a home rule state where municipalities have the right to determine their own processes
for direct democracy. These systems have been built carefully, with input from residents, legal counsel, and generations of precedent. To override them with a statewide mandate not only disrespects that autonomy but suggests that the Legislature does not trust local governments or their voters to govern themselves.
If there are genuine concerns about how referenda are being handled in specific municipalities,
those should be addressed at the local level, in that municipality. Blanket reforms from the State House are not the answer and will only weaken local control, introduce rigidity into processes that require
flexibility, and sow confusion where there is clarity. For these reasons we urge the committee to vote
ought not to pass.
Thank you for your time and for considering the municipal perspective on this issue.
